newsitem.title: YEMEN: Southerners take bitter view of Yemen elections.
newsitem.headline: Southerners take bitter view of Yemen elections.

text.p: Three years after their secession bid was crushed, southern Yemenis are bracing for what could be a deadlier political blow -- the first parliamentary elections since the 1994 civil war.

Yemenis, plagued by years of animosity between north and south, will cast their first parliamentary votes on Sunday since the war hoping that candidates will narrow lingering political divisions and ease economic hardships.

But the main opposition Yemen Socialist Party (YSP), some of whose former leaders launched the southern separatist campaign that sparked the war, and three others have announced they will boycott the poll to protest against alleged irregularities.
President Ali Abdullah Saleh's opponents fear he will tighten his grip on the south.
"Saleh is using the elections to try to spread a blanket of legitimacy on his rule and widen his power over the south," said one opposition member who requested anonymity.
Western diplomats expect Saleh's General People's Congress (GPC) to return as the governing party and some even argue the YSP boycotted the contest to avoid bitter defeat.
"The YSP would have been whitewashed. They lost out in 1994 and they have failed to regroup. The south is left without any real leaders," said one.
Yemen's Minister of Legal and Parliamentary Affairs, Abdullah Ahmad Ghanem, a GPC backer, agrees.

"They (the YSP) know that they will never be able to win a majority. That's why they are boycotting. It's not a matter of irregularities. Yes, there were some irregularities but the government dealt with them," he told Reuters.
Some YSP members will run as independents, a move that has raised concerns among party officials.
A total of 2,306 candidates, including 17 women, are seeking 301 parliamentary seats under the banners of 12 parties or as independents.
The Republic of Yemen was formed in 1990 by the merger of conservative North Yemen and the Marxist south following hundreds of years of separation.

The first general elections in a united Yemen were held in 1993. Since then, some southerners say, the dreams of unity that came with the 1990 merger have been shattered, first by war, and then northern moves to control the south.
Many complain that the government in Sanaa treats the south as a conquered land, rather than an equal part of Yemen.
Saleh rules the south under martial law, southerners are branded permanent traitors and discrimination is rampant, according to the opposition. Sanaa officials deny the charges.

"We just want unity and the government to deliver on its promises of achieving national reconciliation with the south. Instead, we are still labelled as the southern traitors," YSP secretary-general Ali Saleh Obad told Reuters.

Along the dusty streets of the port city of Aden, where young boys in tattered clothes shuffle barefoot past piles of fetid rubbish, the politics of an uneasy unity boil down to the price of bread, meat and milk.
The candidates looking down at Aden from campaign posters promising a better standard of living and political stability do not seem to be allaying daily worries.
"Voting is useless. I can't even afford to buy milk for my family," said a 45-year-old mechanic with four children.
Butchers at the Aden market seem to spend most of their day fighting swarms of flies on their meat.
"Nobody is buying because prices are just too high," said one man, 70-year-old Abdullah.
"The northern government gave us a bad deal. If this goes on there will be another war if God is willing," said another.
For some, the folk songs of a popular Yemeni singer running as an independent candidate seem to offer the only refuge from a bitter past and an uncertain future.
As one of his songs blared from a megaphone mounted on a beaten up car on the campaign trial, a group of women in black veils explained why they are banking on him and not the YSP.
"The YSP's days are over," said Samia Mohammad as her friends nodded in agreement.
